paragraphs: §1 — Sound interpretation must agree with the root; the standard for refutation

We say, before we begin our refutation of them: our scriptures and the words of the prophets may contain that which admits of interpretation (taʾwīl) — yet interpretation is a branch (farʿ) that must be in agreement with the root (aṣl) and not depart from it. As for when the interpretation is at variance with the root and opposed to it, it is known that that interpretation is, beyond doubt, a corrupt interpretation. And since the doctrine of the Christians and their school has had its corruption made plain from the standpoint of reason (min jihat al-maʿqūl) by the decisive proofs, some of which we have already set out, it is established that everything they interpret onto the sayings of Scripture — by which they aim to establish their doctrine, or which agrees with their view — is a corrupt interpretation. Nevertheless, we wish also to make plain the corruption of what they have interpreted from the standpoint of Scripture and language (min jihat al-kitāb wa-l-lugha), so that in that there be the removal of every ambiguity (shubha), and because in some of what they argue there is that which requires explanation and commentary.

: The preamble states Q's two-front method explicitly. The rational refutation (Trinity is incoherent; jawhar / aqānīm / ittiḥād cannot be sustained) was conducted in Babs 1–4; Bab 6 now adds the exegetical-philological refutation. The governing principle — al-taʾwīl farʿ yaḥtāj an yakūn muwāfiqan li-l-aṣl — is a kalām commonplace (the priority of aṣl over farʿ) put to anti-Christian use: a Christological reading that contradicts the plain sense of a verse is ipso facto invalid. This is the same hermeneutical posture Q the Karaite takes against Rabbanite midrash, here turned outward against Christian typology.
§2 — Gen 1:26: naʿaseh is the plural of majesty, and kidmutenu is figurative

As for what they mentioned from the saying of Scripture [Gen 1:26] וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם, and their relying on His saying נַעֲשֶׂה ("let us make"), which is a plural — that is exaltation and magnification (taʿẓīm wa-tafkhīm), just as is used in the language of the Arabs, for the king, the chief, and the noble says "we have commanded," "we have said," "we have done." And likewise Scripture says [Dan 2:36] דְּנָא חֶלְמָא וּפִשְׁרֵהּ נֵאמַר קֳדָם מַלְכָּא ("this is the dream, and we shall tell its interpretation before the king"); and Laban says [Gen 29:27] מַלֵּא שְׁבֻעַ זֹאת וְנִתְּנָה לְּךָ ("fulfill this week and we shall give you"); and Amaziah says [2 Chr 25:17] לְכוּ נִתְרָאֶה פָנִים ("come, let us look one another in the face"); and Job [2:10] גַּם אֶת הַטּוֹב נְקַבֵּל מֵאֵת הָאֱלֹהִים ("shall we accept the good also from God"). And of the same kind is His saying [Gen 1:27 / 5:1] בְּצַלְמוֹ … כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ.

[Then the dialectical squeeze:] It is to be said to the Christians: Inform us — do you hold that this account is in figurative expressions (alfāẓ majāziyya), or that all its expressions are literal and fixed (muḥkama)? If they say that all its expressions are literal, they are obliged to say that Adam is in the image of God in reality, so that the Creator (sublime be His praise) would, on their view, be flesh, bone, sinew, skin, and the rest of what is in a human being — and this they do not say. And they are obliged to say that the Creator is male and female, for His saying [Gen 1:27] בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים בָּרָא אֹתוֹ זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם. And they are obliged to say that all the hypostases (al-aqānīm) created Adam, on account of נַעֲשֶׂה, and that one of them created Eve, on account of His saying [Gen 2:22] וַיִּבֶן ה' אֱלֹהִים — all of which they refuse and reject.

So once they concede that in this account there are figurative expressions — namely that there is here no real form (ṣūra ḥaqīqiyya) and no real likeness, but only the form of an act (ṣūrat fiʿl) and the likeness of an act, as in the saying of one who says "so-and-so is not, in my eyes, of this form," and as one also says "do as resembles you," intending not the form and likeness of the body but the form and likeness of an act — then they are likewise obliged to concede the same regarding all three [hypostases], that is, בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ, and that it is a figure (majāz), as in the saying of one who says "we do and we make, we did and we made," while he alone did and made. And we have already explained, in the Maqala before this one, the meaning of בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ — that being in the refutation of those who hold anthropomorphism (al-tashbīh) — and we have no need to repeat it here.

: The plurale maiestatis reply is the standard Jewish and Karaite answer to the Trinitarian reading of naʿaseh. Q's distinctive move is to ground it not in Hebrew usage alone but cross-linguistically in the royal "we" (qultanā / faʿalnā) of Arabic, then to buttress it with a chain of Hebrew/Aramaic first-person plurals spoken by single human speakers (Daniel before Nebuchadnezzar, Laban, Amaziah, Job). The argument is purely philological: a grammatical plural is not an ontological plural. : This is Q's tu quoque dilemma and the heart of §2. The Christian cannot read Gen 1:26-27 consistently literally without absurdity (a corporeal, sexed, multiply-creating God); so he must concede figurative language somewhere; but once kidmut / ṣelem is granted as figurative ("the likeness of an act," not of a body), the same concession dissolves the ontological-plural reading of naʿaseh. Q's back-reference is to Maqala II's refutation of al-tashbīh (anthropomorphism), where be-tzalmenu ki-dmutenu was already glossed non-corporeally — so he declines to repeat it. The "form of an act, not of a body" (ṣūrat fiʿl lā ṣūrat jism) gloss is the controlling reading.
§3 — Gen 49:10: the ʿad … Shiloh verse, and the two answers of "our colleagues"

As for what they cling to from His saying לֹא יָסוּר שֵׁבֶט מִיהוּדָה — if he intended by it that the kingship shall not depart from the tribe of Judah until the Messiah, who is Jesus, comes, then this is the contrary of what was the case, since the kingship of Judah had departed a long time before the coming of Jesus; and if he intended only the departure of leadership (riʾāsa), then leadership did not depart from them, since the sons of David have been leaders over the house of Israel down to this present time. So here the corruption of their interpretation has not become as plain as it did in the one before it.

If they say: then what is the meaning of his saying that it shall not depart [Gen 49:10] עַד כִּי יָבֹא שִׁילֹה? — if he intended by that the coming of the Messiah whom you await, there are in this two kinds of corruption: the one, that the kingship of Judah departed before his coming, which is the contrary of his saying that it does not depart until he comes; and the second, that the Messiah, in your view, is from Judah, and by his coming the kingship of Judah is established and confirmed — yet his saying "the kingship shall not depart from Judah until the Messiah comes" indicates that at the coming of the Messiah it departs — and this too is a self-contradiction.

We say that our colleagues (aṣḥābunā) have, on this question, two answers. The one: some of them held that his saying עַד כִּי יָבֹא שִׁילֹה intended נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּר, by whose coming the kingship of David departed; he is the one for whom the peoples were struck down, since Scripture says [Jer 28:14] עֹל בַּרְזֶל נָתַתִּי עַל צַוַּאר כָּל הַגּוֹיִם הָאֵלֶּה לַעֲבֹד אֶת נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּר מֶלֶךְ בָּבֶל וַעֲבָדוּהוּ, and His saying [Jer 27:11] וְהַגּוֹי אֲשֶׁר יָבִיא אֶת צַוָּארוֹ and its completion, and He said [Dan 2:38] וּבְכָל דִּי דָארִין בְּנֵי אֲנָשָׁא חֵיוַת בָּרָא וְעוֹף שְׁמַיָּא יְהַב בִּידָךְ.

And others said another saying — and it is the one to which most of our colleagues incline — that the particle עַד indicates two meanings: the one is "until" (ḥattā), and the other is "when / since" (idh); and that is as in His saying [Isa 47:7] וַתֹּאמְרִי לְעוֹלָם אֶהְיֶה גְבָרֶת עַד לֹא שַׂמְתְּ אֵלֶּה עַל לִבֵּךְ, the meaning of which is "since you did not set [these things upon your heart]." They said: when he said "the scepter shall not depart from Judah," [an interlocutor] asked, requesting to be told when this scepter and this enduring king would be; so he said: "when comes the one to whom it belongs" — meaning the Messiah, of whom he informed that his kingship is a firm kingship that does not depart, as Scripture said [Dan 3:33] מַלְכוּתֵיהּ מַלְכוּת עָלַם and [Dan 2:44] יְקִים אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא מַלְכוּ דִּי לְעָלְמִין לָא תִתְחַבַּל.

And we also say that even if the particle עַד had no meaning other than "until," it still would not follow that at the coming of the Messiah, who is שִׁילֹה, that [kingship] departs and is cut off. For when he said that the scepter shall not depart from Judah, [the interlocutor] then asked, requesting to be told until when this promise and bounty would last; so he answered, "until the one to whom it belongs comes." This is comparable to one who promises a man various promises, saying to him, "I shall do thus-and-thus for you, and do thus-and-thus"; and his companion says to him, "until when will you do for me this thing promised?"; and he answers him, saying, "until such-and-such a time, and until such-and-such happens." So his "until" does not intend the cessation of what he promised him, but rather the commencement of his acting on the promise. Just so, his saying עַד כִּי יָבֹא שִׁילֹה does not intend the cessation of the kingship and its departure, but intends the commencement of this kingship of which he informed that it does not depart. And some of our colleagues have, on this point, an interpretation other than these two that we have mentioned, which we shall set out in its place in the last book.

: A candid moment: Q admits that the Gen 49:10 refutation is harder than the Gen 1:26 one — "here the corruption of their interpretation has not become plain as it did in the one before it." The difficulty is real: the verse does seem to predicate an enduring Judahite scepter terminating in a "Shiloh," which invites a messianic reading. Q's honesty in flagging the comparative weakness is characteristic of his Bahshamī-rationalist temper. The Karaite riʾāsa-survives answer (the Davidic exilarchate continued the line) was a live one in Q's Baghdad, where the Exilarch was a Davidide. : Q offers the two standard Karaite construals: (a) Shiloh = Nebuchadnezzar (the scepter "departs" at the Babylonian conquest), and (b) the lexical argument that ʿad can mean "when/since" (Aramaic-influenced ʿad = idh), so the clause marks the inception of the messianic kingship rather than the terminus of the Judahite one. His "promise" analogy (a promiser's "until" naming when fulfilment begins, not when it ends) is a neat pragmatic point about the semantics of temporal ʿad. The "last book" (al-kitāb al-akhīr / al-kitāb al-ākhar) cross-reference recurs through the bab — Q repeatedly defers full treatment to a later work, almost certainly his Torah-commentary, the Kitāb al-Riyāḍ wa-l-Ḥadāʾiq.
§4 — Isa 7:14: ʿalmah means "young woman," the sign is Immanuel-and-Sennacherib, and the Holy-Spirit verses are about prophecy and command

As for what they mentioned from the saying of יְשַׁעְיָהוּ [Isa 7:14] הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה וְיֹלֶדֶת בֵּן, and their flat assertion that this is a birth from no man and no intercourse — that is a claim upon which there is no proof, and in which there is not even an ambiguity, since the jāriya (the maiden) may be a virgin (bikr) or not a virgin. For the meaning of עַלְמָה is the meaning of נַעֲרָה (a young woman), as in His saying [Gen 24:43] וְהָיָה הָעַלְמָה הַיֹּצֵאת לִשְׁאֹב and His saying [Gen 24:14] וְהָיָה הַנַּעֲרָה אֲשֶׁר אֹמַר אֵלֶיהָ; and one who is already married is called עַלְמָה, as in Ruth [4:12] מִן הַזֶּרַע אֲשֶׁר יִתֵּן יְיָ לְךָ מִן הַנַּעֲרָה הַזֹּאת, and as he also says in Proverbs [30:19] וְדֶרֶךְ גֶּבֶר בְּעַלְמָה. So his saying הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה did not intend by it anything that would suggest she is a virgin. Whence, then, did the ignorant ones impose upon us that this birth was from no male and no intercourse?

And there is another aspect also, namely that it is to be said to them: who conceded to you that Mary gave birth from no male and no intercourse? Is this anything but a lying claim with no basis? They would only be entitled to argue from this had it been a matter agreed upon; and this is not among the things in which recourse is had to transmission (naql), since intercourse is a hidden matter, especially for one who had a betrothed (mumlik) — and Joseph the carpenter (Yūsuf al-najjār) was the fiancé (khaṭīb) of Mary and betrothed to her. Indeed, the Jews ascribed Jesus to illegitimacy (ghayr rishda) because Joseph came to his mother Mary while she was betrothed, without sanctifying [the marriage]. And even their own book has reported something resembling this, for it says at the beginning of the Gospels [Matt 1:1] הֲذَا كِتَابُ نِسْبَةِ [يَسُوعَ] الْمَسِيحِ ("this is the book of the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah"); so it made the beginning of the book the genealogy of the Messiah, who is Jesus, then it began and said: "Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob begot Judah," and it kept driving the genealogy down to Joseph the carpenter, the fiancé of Mary, [Luke 3:27] בֶּן שְׁאַלְתִּיאֵל. So since it began and reported that this book is the genealogy of Jesus, then strung the genealogy from Abraham down to Joseph the carpenter who was Mary's fiancé — it necessarily follows from this, beyond doubt, that Jesus is the son of Joseph. And if the matter is not so, then what has Jesus to do with this genealogy? It is rather Joseph's, who [otherwise] has no connection in it. Then it confirmed that by saying that from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the Babylonian exile fourteen generations, and from the Babylonian exile to Jesus fourteen generations.

We return to the saying of Scripture הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה, and we say that from the account itself it becomes plain about whom this was said. For he says at the beginning of the account, "in the days of Ahaz," [Isa 7:11] וַיּוֹסֶף יְיָ … לֵאמֹר שְׁאַל לְךָ אוֹת, and Ahaz said [7:12] לֹא אֶשְׁאַל וְלֹא אֲנַסֶּה אֶת יְיָ; and his refusal of that was not out of reverence for the Creator (exalted be His majesty), nor out of holding [Him] above being tested, but rather by way of denial and dismissal, for he says after it [7:13] וַיֹּאמֶר שִׁמְעוּ נָא בֵּית דָּוִד הַמְעַט מִכֶּם הַלְאוֹת אֲנָשִׁים כִּי תַלְאוּ גַּם אֶת אֱלֹהָי, then he said [7:14] לָכֵן יִתֵּן אֲדֹנָי הוּא לָכֶם אוֹת — that is, even if you do not ask for a sign, God will set up for you a sign, namely that the maiden — meaning his [own] wife — will conceive and bear a son.

If they say: and what sign is there in that? do not all women who have husbands give birth? — we say: two answers are admissible in that. The one: that Ahaz at that time was ten years old, for he begot Hezekiah when he was eleven years old, and it is not the way of a ten-year-old to beget — so this was the sign. The second: it may be that he did not intend, by saying He gives them a sign, what they mentioned of his saying that the maiden conceives and bears, but rather what he appended after that. That is comparable to the saying of God to Moses [Exod 3:12] וְזֶה לְּךָ הָאוֹת כִּי אָנֹכִי שְׁלַחְתִּיךָ בְּהוֹצִיאֲךָ אֶת הָעָם מִמִּצְרַיִם — for his saying "you shall serve God" is not the sign, but something else, namely what preceded of his saying [3:12] כִּי אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ and what was mentioned after it of the miracles He displayed to him. If they say: then what is the sign that he informed he would set up? — we say: it is his saying [Isa 7:15-16] בְּטֶרֶם יֵדַע הַנַּעַר מָאוֹס בָּרָע וּבָחוֹר בַּטּוֹב תֵּעָזֵב הָאֲדָמָה, then he said right after that [7:17] יָבִיא יְיָ עָלֶיךָ וְעַל עַמְּךָ וְעַל בֵּית אָבִיךָ … אֵת מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר, and [8:8] וְחָלַף בִּיהוּדָה, and [8:8] מְלֹא רֹחַב אַרְצְךָ עִמָּנוּ אֵל — so behold, he informs that Sennacherib (סַנְחֵרִיב) will fill your land, O Immanuel. So the ignorant, bewildered ones (al-juhhāl al-ḥayārā) did not read this, and did not grasp that עִמָּנוּאֵל is the one to whose land the king of Assyria comes — and not Jesus, who was a long age after this account. So we seek refuge in God (mighty and exalted) from abandonment.

As for what they clung to from His saying [Isa 48:16] שְׁלָחַנִי וְרוּחוֹ, and that the meaning of that is "God and His spirit sent me" — that too is from their ignorance and their scant acquaintance with the meanings of the language, since the word רוּחַ in Scripture is apportioned over many meanings: among them spirit (rūḥ), wind (rīḥ), command (amr), prophecy (nubuwwa), and other than that. Prophecy is as in His saying [Num 11:25] וְאָצַלְתִּי מִן הָרוּחַ and His saying [11:26] וַתָּנַח עֲלֵיהֶם הָרוּחַ — meaning, prophecy alighted upon them. So his saying שְׁלָחַנִי וְרוּחוֹ means "He sent me and His prophecy," that is, "He sent me and sent His prophecy with me" — not that He and some other thing sent me. As for His saying [Isa 63:10] מָרוּ וְעִצְּבוּ אֶת רוּחַ קָדְשׁוֹ — it means that they opposed His command, which is the command of His holiness; and that is like [Neh 9:20] וְרוּחֲךָ הַטּוֹבָה נָתַתָּ לָהֶם, for His speech is His command. And of the same kind is His saying [2 Sam 23:2] רוּחַ יְיָ דִּבֶּר בִּי וּמִלָּתוֹ — meaning His command and His address, for he says right after it וּמִלָּתוֹ עַל לְשׁוֹנִי.

: Q's ʿalmah argument is the classic philological one (against the LXX/Matthean parthenos = "virgin"): ʿalmah simply denotes a young woman, attested of marriageable and even married women (Gen 24, Ruth 4, Prov 30). He then mounts a sharp ad hominem from the Christians' own genealogies: Matthew (and Luke) trace Jesus' descent through Joseph to David — which is genealogically pointless unless Jesus is Joseph's son, contradicting the virgin-birth claim the Davidic descent is meant to serve. The fourteen-generations schema (Matt 1:17) is cited precisely. The Hebrew-script rendering of Matt 1:1 (hādhā kitāb nisbat … al-masīḥ) is in Arabic in Hebrew letters in the source — Q quotes the Gospel incipit in his own Judeo-Arabic. : The constructive reading: the ʿalmah is Isaiah's own wife, the child a near-term sign to Ahaz, and "Immanuel" the figure whose land Sennacherib's Assyria will overrun (Isa 8:8) — i.e., a contemporary 8th-century referent, decisively not a figure "a long age after." Q's two sub-answers to "what is the sign?" — (a) Ahaz's youth (a chronological midrash: a ten-year-old fathering Hezekiah) and (b) the sign lies in the appended Isa 7:15-17 prophecy, on analogy with Exod 3:12 where the "sign" is the sequel, not the immediate statement — are both standard in the Karaite Isaiah commentaries (cf. Yefet ben ʿEli ad loc.). The Exod 3:12 parallel (the sign is future deliverance, not the present utterance) is exegetically deft. : The Holy-Spirit trio is dispatched by the polysemy of rûaḥ: it can mean spirit, wind, command, or prophecy. "He sent me and His rûaḥ" = "He sent me and His prophecy with me" (Num 11:25-26 supplying the rûaḥ = prophecy sense); "they grieved His holy rûaḥ" = they defied His command (Neh 9:20 parallel); "the rûaḥ of the Lord spoke in me" = His command/address, confirmed by the synonymous u-millato ʿal leshoni ("and His word upon my tongue") in the same verse. In each case Q's point is that rûaḥ is not a distinct hypostasis but a polysemous noun whose contextual sense is "command/prophecy."
§5 — [The Holy-Spirit verses, treated above, complete the Isa-cluster refutation]
§6 — Ps 2:7, Ps 2:12, Ps 110:1: "son" means "beloved," and the messianic Psalms do not fit Jesus

As for their clinging to His saying [Ps 2:7] כִּי אָמַר אֵלַי בְּנִי אַתָּה and His saying [Ps 2:12] נַשְּׁקוּ בַר פֶּן יֶאֱנַף — not everyone who is named בֵּן ("son") is a [literal] son, since all the house of Israel, in their entirety, have been named בָּנִים, on account of His saying [Deut 14:1] בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַיהוָה — the meaning of which is not "[biological] sons," for he only intended by it "beloved ones / clients" (awliyāʾ). Likewise His saying [Exod 4:22] בְּנִי בְכֹרִי יִשְׂרָאֵל refers to the Messiah whom we [Jews] await, for he says after it [Ps 2:7-9] אֲנִי הַיּוֹם יְלִדְתִּיךָ שְׁאַל מִמֶּנִּי וְאֶתְּנָה גוֹיִם נַחֲלָתֶךָ … תְּרֹעֵם בְּשֵׁבֶט בַּרְזֶל — and Jesus never had any of this at all; he was rather lowly, despised, and contemptible, until he was killed and crucified. As for the saying of Scripture [Ps 110:1] נְאֻם יְיָ לַאדֹנִי — it is the counterpart of what preceded, namely that God said to the Messiah שֵׁב לִימִינִי, meaning: be firmly established upon the ordinance of the Torah, which is named by that [right-hand imagery], on account of His saying [Deut 33:2] … מִימִינוֹ אֵשׁ דָּת לָמוֹ ("from His right hand a fiery law for them").

: The Father-Son verses are met with the same lexical strategy: ben in Scripture often denotes the beloved/client (walī), not a biological son — Deut 14:1 ("you are sons to the Lord") and Exod 4:22 ("Israel my firstborn son") prove the figurative range. Q then turns Ps 2 against the Christians historically: its imperial promises (the nations as inheritance, the iron scepter) manifestly never applied to the crucified Jesus, but await the (Jewish) Messiah. The reading of Ps 110:1's shev li-mini ("sit at my right") as "be established on the Torah-ordinance" via the yamin/esh dat link of Deut 33:2 is a distinctively Karaite legal-typological move — even the royal-enthronement Psalm is bent back toward Torah-observance, the controlling Karaite value.
§7 — Ps 56:11: even on the Christian rendering, davar is ordinary speech, not the eternal Word

As for what they clung to concerning the Word (al-kalima) and the saying of Scripture [Ps 56:11] בֵּאלֹהִים אֲהַלֵּל דָּבָר — some of our colleagues interpret it otherwise than they do, and hold that its meaning is "in God I praise my affair (amrī)." But we proceed only upon [the supposition] that its interpretation is as they themselves have said, namely "by the Word I praise God." [Even so,] there is in this nothing that indicates the pre-eternity of the Word (qidam al-kalima), since we praise God and glorify Him and magnify Him by the speech (al-kalām) that is prayer and glorification.

: A concessive argument (even granting your rendering): Q sets aside the Karaite construal of davar as "my affair/matter" and adopts the Christian rendering "by the davar I praise God" — and shows that it still yields nothing, because "word/speech" here is simply the human speech of prayer and praise, not a pre-eternal Logos. This connects back to Bab 3's refutation of qidam al-kalima (the eternity of the Word): even the Christians' best verse cannot establish a hypostatized eternal Word.
§8 — Deut 10:12 and Mic 6:8: "fear" and "humility" presuppose the commandments

As for their argument that the ordinances of the Torah are not pleasing, and that what God wants from people is only fear (al-khashiya) and humility (al-tawāḍuʿ) — by His saying [Deut 10:12] וְעַתָּה יִשְׂרָאֵל … and His saying כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה אֶת ה', and His saying in Micah [6:8] וּמָה ה' דּוֹרֵשׁ מִמְּךָ etc. — do the ignorant, bewildered ones not know that fear (al-khashiya) is realized only through the acceptance of command and prohibition and the fearing of promise and threat? For he says, right after his saying כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה: וְלָלֶכֶת בִּדְרָכָיו ("and to walk in His ways"), and again the walking אַחֲרֵי יְיָ אֱלֹהֶיךָ — and walking in His paths is the doing of what He commanded and the refraining from what He forbade, since [Scripture] says of Abraham [Gen 18:19] כִּי יְדַעְתִּיו לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה אֶת בָּנָיו … and says [same place] וְשָׁמְרוּ דֶּרֶךְ יְיָ, meaning His ordinances, just as Jeremiah said [Jer 5:5] אֵלְכָה לִּי אֶל הַגְּדֹלִים וַאֲדַבְּרָה אוֹתָם כִּי הֵמָּה יָדְעוּ דֶּרֶךְ יְיָ.

And of the same kind is his saying in Micah [6:8] דּוֹרֵשׁ מִמְּךָ כִּי אִם עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט — for he did not confine himself in it to mentioning humility alone, which is וְהַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת עִם אֱלֹהֶיךָ, but rather sealed the statement with that after he had first put forward the mention of the ordinances; and that is in his saying כִּי אִם עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט וְאַהֲבַת חֶסֶד — and that [mishpat] is the ordinance, since [Exod 21:1] וְאֵלֶּה הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים אֲשֶׁר תָּשִׂים לִפְנֵיהֶם; and David (peace be upon him) says [Ps 19:8] תּוֹרַת יְיָ תְּמִימָה מְשִׁיבַת נָפֶשׁ — and that, beyond doubt, is the Torah and its ordinances — then he sealed that by saying [Ps 19:10] מִשְׁפְּטֵי יְיָ אֱמֶת. And Malachi, when mentioning the last of the affairs of the kingdoms and the states, says [Mal 3:22] זִכְרוּ תּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה עַבְדִּי, and says [same place] חֻקִּים וּמִשְׁפָּטִים. So even were there upon them only this single transgression [of neglecting the law], there would be in it a demolition (hadm) of everything they claim, since it is stated regarding what He wants to be at the expiry of the states and kingdoms, and at the time in which אֵלִיָּהוּ (peace be upon him) is sent — [namely] that He made obligatory the remembrance of the Torah; and its remembrance is the acting by it and by the ordinances, command, prohibition, and judgments within it. And in this transgression-passage is a refutation of everyone who claims the abrogation (naskh) of the ordinances of the Torah and their nullity.

: The pivot of the anti-legal refutation: the very verses adduced against the law in fact embed it. "To fear" (Deut 10:12) is immediately glossed by Scripture itself as "to walk in His ways" = to keep command and prohibition (Gen 18:19's derekh YHWH = His ordinances). In Mic 6:8 the order is decisive: "do justice (mishpat) and love mercy" precedes "walk humbly" — and mishpat is a technical term for legal ordinance (Exod 21:1). Q clinches it eschatologically with Mal 3:22-24: the very prophet who speaks of the end-time sending of Elijah commands "remember the Torah of Moses … statutes and ordinances" — so the law is operative at the eschaton, and any claim of naskh (abrogation, the Islamic term Q borrows) is demolished (hadm).
§9 — The king (1 Sam 8): a permission conditioned on Israel's request, not a command

As for their clinging to the matter of the king — that too is from the excess of their ignorance, since that was not an ordinance, nor did He command them to set up a king; rather He said to them: when you say "we will set over ourselves a king like the rest of the nations," then set up the one whom God chooses. This is plain, beyond needing to be expanded upon; and we shall explain this account in its place in the other book.

: Brief, because the point is clean: Deut 17:15 is not a command to appoint a king but a regulation of a permitted contingency ("when you say…, then…"). God's displeasure in 1 Sam 8 is therefore not displeasure at a commanded thing, but at the faithless manner of the request — so the Christian "a commanded thing can be displeasing" inference collapses. Again deferred to "the other book" for full treatment.
§10 — The sacrifices: three classes of offering; Jer 7:22 concerns only the voluntary kind

As for the matter of the offering (al-qurbān), and the transgression-passages that occur in it that suggest the Creator did not command it — the answer regarding that is that the offerings are of three classes. Among them is that which is commanded as a standing [obligation] (qāʾiman), which inevitably must be performed, and which has no cause necessitating it except the very arrival of the time in which one is bound to worship by performing it — and that is like the תָּמִיד offering, which is at morning and at evening, and likewise the offering of the Sabbath, of the new moons, and of the festivals. And among them is that which is obligatory on account of a cause that arises — and that is like the offering of the נִדָּה (menstruant), and the יוֹלֵדָה (woman who has given birth), and the זָבָה, and the like of that; for this becomes obligatory only by the event that arises, and when that event does not occur, its performance is not obligatory. And among them is that which is not obligatory at all, but is rather something a person chooses to perform — if he wishes he performs it, and if he wishes he does not — and that is like the נֶדֶר וּנְדָבָה וְתוֹדָה (vow, freewill offering, thank-offering), which are not obligatory, but are rather a person's voluntary act: if he wishes he vows, and if he wishes he does not vow.

So it is admissible that what Scripture mentioned in His saying [Jer 7:22] כִּי לֹא דִבַּרְתִּי אֶת אֲבוֹתֵיכֶם וְלֹא צִוִּיתִים and the rest of what resembles that refers to this [third] class, which is the one of choice and voluntary [offering] — to the exclusion of the rest of the prescribed offerings, since Scripture has [explicitly] stipulated their obligation, and the Sage (al-ḥakīm) does not contradict [Himself]. This is one aspect.

: The threefold taxonomy — (1) fixed/calendrical (tamid, Sabbath, festivals); (2) contingent/occasioned (purificatory offerings of the niddah, yoledet, zavah); (3) wholly voluntary (neder, nedavah, todah) — lets Q quarantine Jer 7:22 to class (3): God "did not command" precisely the voluntary offerings, so the verse, far from denying that sacrifice was commanded, is consistent with the obligatory classes being commanded. The clinching premise is al-ḥakīm lā yunāqiḍ ("the Wise One does not contradict Himself") — a rationalist axiom that forbids reading one verse to abrogate the explicit legislation of another.
§11 — Sacrifice is rejected only when offered alongside sin; it is restored at the future temple

And [there is] another aspect, namely that we have found Scripture, in many places, informing that the offerings are obligatory to perform only together with the perfection of [acts of] obedience, and that thereby they are accepted; but that when they are offered together with acts of disobedience, they are not pleasing and not accepted, but rather hateful. Of that is the saying of יְשַׁעְיָהוּ, after he had mentioned their evil deeds, for he said [Isa 1:11] לָמָּה לִּי רֹב זִבְחֵיכֶם יֹאמַר יְיָ etc., and his saying [1:13] לֹא תוֹסִיפוּ הָבִיא מִנְחַת שָׁוְא; and likewise the saying of the Creator in another place [Amos 5:22] כִּי אִם תַּעֲלוּ לִי עֹלוֹת וּמִנְחֹתֵיכֶם לֹא אֶרְצֶה etc., and His saying also [Mal 1:10] וּמִנְחָה לֹא אֶרְצֶה מִיֶּדְכֶם, and His saying [Jer 6:20] עֹלֹתֵיכֶם לֹא לְרָצוֹן — and all of that is on account of sins and offenses.

And for this cause He said [Isa 66:3] שׁוֹחֵט הַשּׁוֹר מַכֵּה אִישׁ etc. For He said at the beginning of the account [Isa 66:1] כֹּה אָמַר יְיָ הַשָּׁמַיִם כִּסְאִי … וְאֶת כָּל אֵלֶּה יָדִי עָשָׂתָה etc., then He said [66:2] וְאֶל זֶה אַבִּיט אֶל עָנִי וּנְכֵה רוּחַ וְחָרֵד עַל דְּבָרִי — informing that He seeks and turns only to one who is humble, submissive, lowly, anxious toward His speech, which is His command and His prohibition, taking up obedience to Him and forsaking disobedience to Him. Then He said שׁוֹחֵט הַשּׁוֹר מַכֵּה אִישׁ — that is, whoever this was not his way, but was rather disobedient, then came offering an offering and slaughtered a bull, it is as though he had killed a man — along with the rest of what He mentioned. Then He confirmed that and made it plain by His saying [Isa 66:3] גַּם הֵמָּה בָּחֲרוּ בְּדַרְכֵיהֶם — that is, that they, despite this menacing and these warnings, did not desist from the acts of disobedience they were in, but rather chose them and plunged into them.

And the argument is against whoever attaches to the matter of the offerings and claims that He commanded it out of wrath, and that it is not pleasing — and did not look into the saying of יְחֶזְקֵאל at the end of his mention of the building of the future temple, and his saying [Ezek 43:27] וְכִלּוּ אֶת הַיָּמִים וְהָיָה בַיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי וָהָלְאָה יַעֲשׂוּ הַכֹּהֲנִים עַל הַמִּזְבֵּחַ אֶת עוֹלֹתֵיכֶם etc., and its completion — for he informed that at the coming of the deliverance of the house of Israel, and the building of the temple, and the extinction of all the nations, the priests will offer the offerings, and God will be pleased with His nation. And of the same kind is the saying of מַלְאָכִי [3:4] וְעָרְבָה לַיְיָ מִנְחַת יְהוּדָה וִירוּשָׁלָםִ etc.

: The second sacrificial argument neutralizes the prophetic "I hate your sacrifices" topos (Isa 1, Amos 5, Mal 1, Jer 6): these reject sacrifice offered alongside unrepented sin, not sacrifice as such — Isa 66:1-3 makes the conditionality explicit (God turns to the contrite; the bull-slaughterer who persists in sin is "as one who kills a man"). Q then deploys the eschatological clincher he will use repeatedly through §§14-18: Ezekiel's future-temple vision (Ezek 43:27) and Mal 3:4 both restore sacrificial worship in the redeemed age — proof that the cult is not abolished but pleasing-when-rightly-offered.
§12 — Jer 31:31: the "new covenant" confirms the Torah; it differs only in Israel's protected obedience

As for their argument that the ordinances of the Torah have been abrogated and have ceased, by His saying [Jer 31:31] הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים נְאֻם יְיָ וְכָרַתִּי אֶת בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֶת בֵּית יְהוּדָה בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה לֹא כַבְּרִית אֲשֶׁר כָּרַתִּי אֶת אֲבוֹתָם — there is no proof more indicative than it of the establishment of the ordinances of the Torah, and their bindingness, and their perpetuation. And that is plain from the meaning itself, for he says at the end of the passage [Jer 31:32] נָתַתִּי אֶת תּוֹרָתִי בְּקִרְבָּם וְעַל לִבָּם אֶכְתֳּבֶנָּה etc. — and that is the meaning of his saying בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה, since there is no Torah and no covenant except the Torah of Moses and the covenant that was at Sinai and at חוֹרֵב.

So his saying "a new covenant" — he intended by it that the first covenant had after it a breaking (nakth); we know this from his saying [31:32] אֲשֶׁר הֵמָּה הֵפֵרוּ אֶת בְּרִיתִי — whereas the second covenant, which is to come, has no breaking after it. And perhaps one might say: but is not the breaking and the not-breaking [Israel's] own act and choice? The answer is: yes, that is so. If he says: then, if that is so, what is the thing that He does, since He only informs that He will cut a new covenant? — we say: the people, in the first matter, were left to themselves and to their ignorance and the blindness of their hearts, neither preserved nor rightly-guided, and the trials were loosed upon them, and nothing was placed between them and the acts of disobedience; and it may be that the cause necessitating that for them was the evil of their intentions, on account of His saying [Ezek 14:5] לְמַעַן תְּפֹשׂ אֶת בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּלִבָּם etc., and His saying [Isa 29:13] וְרִחַק לִבּוֹ מִמֶּנִּי, and the like of that is much. And in this second, promised matter — contrary to the first — their hearts are cleared, their minds are made pure, ignorance is lifted from them, wisdom is multiplied among them, and they become preserved and rightly-guided. That is known from several places, among them His saying [Ezek 36:26] וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת לֵב הָאֶבֶן and its completion, and His saying [36:27] וְאֶת רוּחִי אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם וְעָשִׂיתִי אֵת אֲשֶׁר בְּחֻקַּי תֵּלֵכוּ etc., and His saying [Jer 32:40] וְאֶת יִרְאָתִי אֶתֵּן בִּלְבָבָם, and His saying [Jer 31:33] וְלֹא יְלַמְּדוּ עוֹד אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ וְאִישׁ אֶת אָחִיו etc.

And it is admissible that the matter necessitating that for them is the opposite of the first — namely purity of heart and soundness of intention — the counterpart of His saying [Deut 30:6] וּמָל ה' אֶת לְבָבְךָ וְאֶת לְבַב זַרְעֶךָ. This is not the place for the exhaustive treatment of this discourse; we have treated it exhaustively in the discussion against the Mujbira (the Compulsionists), that being in the commentary on בְּרֵאשִׁית. But from this very meaning that we have mentioned, it is made plain that his saying בְּרִית מֶלַח and his saying לֹא כָבְתָה intended nothing but what we have said.

: The "new covenant" verse — the Christian abrogation prooftext (and the source of "New Testament," kainē diathēkē) — is turned 180°: Jer 31:32's continuation, "I will put my Torah within them," shows the "new covenant" is the Torah of Moses (the only covenant there is), now internalized. What is "new" is not the law's content but Israel's relation to it: in the first covenant Israel was left morally unaided and so broke it; in the second, hearts of stone are removed (Ezek 36:26-27) and obedience is divinely secured (Jer 32:40, Deut 30:6's circumcised heart). The aside on whether obedience is "their own act and choice" engages the free-will/predestination question Q treats fully contra the Mujbira (the predestinarian Compulsionists) "in the commentary on Bereshit" — another cross-reference to his Torah commentary.
§13 — Dan 9:24-26: the "seventy weeks" refute the Christians from three directions; yikkaret is not unjust killing

As for what they adduced as a ground from His saying [Dan 9:26] וְאַחֲרֵי הַשָּׁבֻעִים שִׁשִּׁים וּשְׁנַיִם יִכָּרֵת מָשִׁיחַ, and [their claim] that this indicates that the Messiah has [already] come and passed, and that he is the one who was killed — since it says of him יִכָּרֵת מָשִׁיחַ — [we reply that] since he had earlier put forward his saying [Dan 9:25] וְתֵדַע וְתַשְׂכֵּל מִן מֹצָא דָבָר לְהָשִׁיב וְלִבְנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם עַד מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד, it corrupts their statement from more than one direction.

The first of them: his saying [9:25] עַד מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד שָׁבֻעִים שִׁבְעָה — for he informed that the מָשִׁיחַ נָגִיד comes after seven weeks, which are forty-nine years; so if this is Jesus, then Jesus must have appeared after [only] fifty years from the building of the temple — and this is false. The second: that he said וְאַחֲרֵי הַשָּׁבֻעִים שִׁשִּׁים וּשְׁנַיִם יִכָּרֵת — so he informed, on their view, that he is killed after sixty-two weeks; so Jesus must have lived something over four hundred years — and this too is the utmost of the absurd and the contradictory. The third: that the word יִכָּרֵת in all of Scripture falls only on two meanings — either the cutting-off of the thing spoken of, or a killing by [legal] desert (qatl bi-stiḥqāq) — and that is as in [Num 15:31] הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִיא … וְנִכְרְתָה and His saying [Exod 30:33] וְנִכְרַת מֵעַמָּיו, and the like of that; but it does not fall on a killing by injustice (qatl bi-ẓulm). So if his saying יִכָּרֵת מָשִׁיחַ intended by it the killing of Jesus, then he was deserving of the killing that befell him, and that is what is intended! — [a conclusion the Christians cannot accept].

And that which Scripture intended by his saying יִכָּרֵת מָשִׁיחַ [is] the cutting-off of the anointing (al-masūḥiyya) — meaning the כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל (the high priest), of whom it is said [Num 35:25] אֲשֶׁר מָשַׁח אֹתוֹ בְּשֶׁמֶן הַקֹּדֶשׁ — that is, from that time on, no high priest is anointed. And that too is plain from the meaning itself, for he says [Dan 9:27] וַחֲצִי שָׁבוּעַ יַשְׁבִּית זֶבַח וּמִנְחָה — for it was in the context of the mention of the offerings, the bloods, and the like of that.

: A three-pronged refutation of the Christian reading of Daniel's "anointed one cut off." (1) and (2) are chronological reductiones: taking the "weeks" as Jesus' lifespan forces either a 50-years-after-rebuilding appearance or a 400-year lifespan. (3) is the philological master-stroke: yikkaret in biblical usage means either cessation of a thing or judicial execution/excision (Num 15:31, Exod 30:33 — the karet penalty), never killing-by-injustice. So if the Christians insist yikkaret mashiaḥ = the killing of Jesus, they impale themselves: it would make Jesus a justly executed criminal. Q's own reading: mashiaḥ = the anointed high priest, and the verse foretells the cessation of the anointing and the sacrificial cult (confirmed by 9:27's "he shall cause sacrifice and offering to cease"). The clever turning of the opponent's prooftext into a self-incrimination is vintage Q.
§14 — Ezekiel's temple was not the Second Temple: the uncircumcised hold Jerusalem, yet the prophecy bars them

As for what they claimed of the building of the temple of which יְחֶזְקֵאל informed — that it is the Second Temple mentioned [in the days] of עֶזְרָא (peace be upon him) and none other, and that all the promises which Scripture promised would come at the coming of the deliverer (al-fārūq) have [already] been fulfilled, and have passed and elapsed — that is calumny (baht) and impudence (qiḥḥa); and a people of those who are firm in the religion [i.e., some Jews] have shared with them in that.

Among that which nullifies the statement of the Christians in particular in this [matter] is the saying of Scripture [Isa 52:1] עוּרִי עוּרִי לִבְשִׁי עֻזֵּךְ צִיּוֹן לִבְשִׁי בִּגְדֵי תִפְאַרְתֵּךְ יְרוּשָׁלַ͏ִם עִיר הַקֹּדֶשׁ כִּי לֹא יוֹסִיף יָבֹא בָךְ עוֹד עָרֵל וְטָמֵא ("for no more shall the uncircumcised and the impure enter you"). For it is to be said to them: is not the ordinance of circumcision, in your view, not obligatory — and are you not, all of you, uncircumcised (qulf)? There is no escape from [saying] "yes." It is then said: how can it be that the promised temple has [already] been fulfilled and elapsed, when along with the promises, the good tidings, and the building of the temple it was informed that צִיּוֹן — no uncircumcised one and no impure one enters it — while there were in it the Romans (al-Rūm), who are all of them uncircumcised, and part of it is also in their hands, and you [too] are uncircumcised? And is there in argument anything more forceful than this?

: The first of the "temple not yet built" arguments turns on a present-day empirical fact: Isa 52:1 promises that no uncircumcised or impure person will enter redeemed Zion — yet the (uncircumcised) Romans/Byzantines (al-Rūm) held and partly hold Jerusalem. So the prophecy is manifestly unfulfilled; the redeemed Jerusalem is future. al-fārūq ("the deliverer/discriminator") here is Q's term for the awaited redeemer-figure whose coming the promises are pinned to. baht (mendacity/calumny) and qiḥḥa (brazen impudence) are Q's recurring polemical register for Christian apologetic — catalogued in the glossary's §IX.
§15 — The "foreskin of the heart" evasion fails twice over: unqualified ʿarel means bodily; and the Muslims hold the city

So some of them contrive, to answer this question, by claiming that "the foreskin" [intends] the heart, so that his saying עָרֵל וְטָמֵא intended by it the uncircumcised of heart. In this answer there are two kinds of rebuttal.

The one: that when Scripture wishes to mention the foreskin of the heart, it must conjoin with mentioning it the mention of the heart; and when it mentions foreskin absolutely (muṭlaqa), it intends by it nothing other than the foreskin of the male organ, to the exclusion of any other — for it says [Jer 9:25] … כָּל מוּל בְּעָרְלָה כִּי כָל הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים, meaning by it the uncircumcised of the male organ, so it said that absolutely, without conjoining anything to it; but when it wished to mention the foreskin of the heart it said כָּל הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים וְכָל בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל עַרְלֵי לֵב. So when it said here עַרְלֵי לֵב [explicitly], and [elsewhere] left [the word] unqualified in an absolute statement, we knew that by [the absolute usage] it intended only the uncircumcised of the male organ.

And the other kind is that it is said to them: is not the foreskin of the heart the abandonment of faith, and the holding of a doctrine that is not true, and a religion that is not sound? When they say "yes," it is said to them: if His saying כִּי לֹא יוֹסִיף יָבוֹא בָךְ עוֹד עָרֵל וְטָמֵא intended by it the uncircumcised of heart, as you have mentioned — and the temple and the town, which were promised that this would belong to them, had [already] been and were built, and it is not a matter that is to come but has [already] been carried out — then, after the completion of the promise, there ought not to enter it any unbeliever or any opponent. So why has it come to be in the hands of the Muslims (al-Muslimīn), and they enter it and possess it, and they are the ones in control of it to the exclusion of others — while they are, in your view, the worst of God's creation in the matter of religion, and the blindest of them in heart? And this is among the most indicative of proofs for nullifying what you claim — namely that this statement and this good tiding have [already] been fulfilled and have run their course; rather they are still to come anew, and have not [yet] arrived.

And of that which also corrupts what they have interpreted in that [matter] is what יְחֶזְקֵאל (peace be upon him) informed, when mentioning and describing the building of the future temple, and what will come of the return of the nation and its state, in his saying [Ezek 44:9] כָּל בֶּן נֵכָר עֶרֶל לֵב וְעֶרֶל בָּשָׂר לֹא יָבוֹא אֶל מִקְדָּשִׁי etc. — for he specified both the possessors of the two foreskins, the foreskin of the flesh and the foreskin of the heart, that they do not enter the temple after its building. So this is a decisive proof and a binding text that the Second Temple, which was built in the days of עֶזְרָא, is not the one which יְחֶזְקֵאל saw and informed would be built — since both classes [the uncircumcised of flesh and of heart] did enter it after its building.

: Q anticipates and demolishes the Christian rejoinder that "uncircumcised" in Isa 52:1 is metaphorical ("uncircumcised of heart"). (1) A philological rule: when Scripture means heart-foreskin, it says "heart" (Jer 9:25's contrast between unqualified ʿarelim = bodily, and ʿarlei lev = of heart); unqualified ʿarel is always bodily. (2) An empirical coup de grâce: even granting the metaphorical reading (uncircumcised-of-heart = false-believers), the Muslims — "the worst of God's creation in religion," on the Christian view — now rule Jerusalem; so the prophecy that no such person enters redeemed Zion is still unfulfilled. Ezek 44:9 seals it by barring both foreskins from the future sanctuary, which the Second Temple admitted — hence Ezekiel's temple ≠ the Second Temple. Note Q's deadpan use of the Christians' own contempt for Islam against them.
§16 — Joy promised vs. weeping at the founding; and the debate with Bishop Yashūʿ Paddā of ʿUkbarā

And among the proofs also that the temple and the promises of which יְשַׁעְיָהוּ (peace be upon him) and others informed had not [yet] been and not [yet] come is his saying [Isa 65:19] וְגַלְתִּי בִירוּשָׁלַ͏ִם וְשַׂשְׂתִּי בְעַמִּי וְלֹא יִשָּׁמַע בָּהּ עוֹד קוֹל בְּכִי וְקוֹל זְעָקָה ("there shall no more be heard in it the sound of weeping and the sound of crying"). Yet we found him saying, regarding the building of the Second Temple [Ezra 3:12] וְרַבִּים מֵהַכֹּהֲנִים וְהַלְוִיִּם וְרָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת הַזְּקֵנִים אֲשֶׁר רָאוּ אֶת הַבַּיִת הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּיָסְדוֹ זֶה הַבַּיִת בְּעֵינֵיהֶם בֹּכִים בְּקוֹל גָּדוֹל, and he says [Ezra 3:13] וְאֵין הָעָם מַכִּירִים קוֹל תְּרוּעַת הַשִּׂמְחָה לְקוֹל בְּכִי הָעָם — and this is like the first, and worse. And he says in another place [Neh 5:1] וַתְּהִי צַעֲקַת הָעָם וּנְשֵׁיהֶם גְּדוֹלָה etc.

And I once asked, of a bishop who was in ʿUkbarā (named Yashūʿ Paddā, and he was among the eminent of the bishops and their scholars), about this question; and he said to me that what was informed [in those verses] was the narration of a report from לְאַדְרָא, and that it may be that it had no basis. And I sought to probe his reason, for I had not seen, among the scholars of the Christians and their men of inquiry, any of less calumny (baht) than he — for as for the rest of them, calumny is their stock-in-trade. So this one too, when the matter compelled him, found no escape from resorting to calumny. I then said to him at that point: is there, then, any proof that the temple was [in fact] built? He did no more than smile, and said to me: "By your honesty — it was not built." So I knew that he had been pressed by that with which I intended to bind him. Then I made it explicit by saying to him: the report from which we know that the temple was built is recorded only in לְאַדְרָא; so if some of what is in לְאַדְרָא may be a lie with no basis, then nothing in it is trustworthy, and so the report that the temple was built would [equally] be a lie with no basis. And he did not utter a single letter [in reply].

: A rare autobiographical vignette and a sharp dialectical trap. Q sets a contradiction: Isaiah promises no more weeping in redeemed Jerusalem (Isa 65:19), yet Ezra 3:12-13 and Neh 5:1 record weeping at the Second Temple's founding — so the Second Temple is not the promised one. His Christian interlocutor, Bishop Yashūʿ Paddā of ʿUkbarā (a real Baghdad-region town with an East-Syrian Christian presence), tries to defuse it by impugning the source of the weeping report — "it may have no basis" — whereupon Q springs the trap: that same source (לְאַדְרָא — most plausibly an Aramaic book-name, perhaps the records/tradition, the deuterocanonical Ezra-material, or a Diatessaron-adjacent text) is also the only witness that the temple was rebuilt at all; impugn it and you lose your own evidence. The bishop's silence is Q's rhetorical victory. Q's backhanded compliment ("the least mendacious Christian scholar I met") is characteristic of the bab's polemical register.
§17 — The measurements: Ezekiel's temple dwarfs the Second Temple, and is never to be destroyed

And among the proofs of that also is what He informed, in [the book of] יְחֶזְקֵאל (peace be upon him), of the measurement of the temple which he said he saw and which He intends shall come to be — and its largeness and immensity, whose magnitude is manifold multiples over the temple that שְׁלֹמֹה (peace be upon him) built; whereas they inform that the temple which was built in the days of עֶזְרָא (peace be upon him) was only upon its former dimension, on account of His saying [Ezra 5:16] וּבְנָיֵת אֱלָהָא דְנָא עַל אַתְרֵהּ ("and this house of God was built upon its [former] site"). So how can it be admissible for the ignorant to say that this [Second Temple] is the one of which יְחֶזְקֵאל (peace be upon him) informed — were it not for the excess of obstinacy? And of that also is what He informed: that the promised temple, together with the rest of the city, shall never be ruined — since He says [Jer 31:40] וְכָל הָעֵמֶק הַפְּגָרִים וְהַדֶּשֶׁן … and He says [same place] לֹא יִנָּתֵשׁ וְלֹא יֵהָרֵס עוֹד לְעוֹלָם ("it shall never again be uprooted or overthrown, forever").

: Two more disqualifiers of the Second-Temple identification: (a) scale — Ezekiel's visionary temple (Ezek 40-43) is vastly larger than Solomon's, whereas the Second Temple was rebuilt merely "on its [former] site" at its old dimensions (Ezra 5:16); and (b) permanence — the promised temple and city are "never again to be uprooted or overthrown" (Jer 31:40), yet the Second Temple was destroyed (70 CE). Both facts force the visionary temple into the unrealized future.
§18 — At the future temple the festivals bind all nations and the dietary laws stand — so the law is not abrogated; transition to Bab 7

Then it is to be said to them: you claim that by the coming of Jesus, who in your view is the Messiah, the ordinances of the Torah fall; and you claim, along with that, that the temple of which יְחֶזְקֵאל informed that it would be has [already] been fulfilled and has elapsed. Yet we have seen זְכַרְיָה (peace be upon him) inform that at the building of the temple the nations will make the pilgrimage [for] חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת (the Festival of Booths), and that whoever falls short of that, the smiting befalls him — on account of his saying [Zech 14:16-18] וְהָיָה הַמַּגֵּפָה אֲשֶׁר יִגֹּף יְיָ אֶת כָּל הַגּוֹיִם אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַעֲלוּ לָחֹג אֶת חַג הַסֻּכּוֹת. So he informs that the ordinance — which is the ordinance of the Torah — at the building of the temple becomes binding upon all the nations; while you claim that it falls away. What calumny, then, suffices for this?

And of the same kind, יְחֶזְקֵאל says regarding the festival of unleavened bread [Ezek 45:21] יִהְיֶה לָכֶם הַפֶּסַח חַג שְׁבֻעוֹת יָמִים מַצּוֹת יֵאָכֵל; and likewise what he mentioned of the offerings, and of the increase in them over what had preceded — such as [Ezek 46:4-5] וְהָעֹלָה אֲשֶׁר יַקְרִיב הַנָּשִׂיא לַיְיָ בְּיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת שִׁשָּׁה כְבָשִׂים etc.; and of the same kind is the saying of יְשַׁעְיָהוּ [66:23] וְהָיָה מִדֵּי חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ וּמִדֵּי שַׁבָּת בְּשַׁבַּתּוֹ etc. — for he informs, right after his mention of the good tidings and the promises which you claim have [already] been fulfilled, that all creation comes to pray before Him in the Sanctuary at the new moons and on the days of the Sabbaths.

And he also informs, in this [same] account, of the censure of the eaters of swine's flesh and of others of the forbidden things — that they perish and are cut off — that being in his saying [Isa 66:17] אֹכְלֵי בְּשַׂר הַחֲזִיר וְהַשֶּׁקֶץ וְהָעַכְבָּר יַחְדָּו יָסֻפוּ נְאֻם יְיָ — while you claim that all animals, swine and others, were released and their eating became permitted by the coming of Jesus. So does one in whom there is the least sense advance such a statement, let alone one who lays claim to knowledge and inquiry?

And since we said that a people of those who profess our religion [i.e., some Jews] have shared with them [the Christians] in the statement that the temple promised to be built has [already] elapsed and been fulfilled, and likewise all the good tidings — we shall, after this, also examine that which corrupts the statement of all [of them]. And we wish now to mention and make plain what we promised of mentioning that which is in Scripture that necessitates the eternal reward and punishment (al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb al-abadī) — that which the Christians spoke of, and claimed has no trace in Scripture.

: The closing argument and the bridge to Bab 7. Q marshals the eschatological prophecies one last time: Zech 14:16-18 makes Sukkot binding on all nations at the redemption (with plague for non-compliance); Ezek 45:21 keeps Passover; Ezek 46:4-5 keeps Sabbath offerings; Isa 66:23 keeps new-moon and Sabbath worship; and Isa 66:17 keeps the dietary prohibitions (swine, vermin) in force in the redeemed age. Since the redemption retains the law in full, the Christian claim of naskh is incoherent. The final sentence pivots to Bab 7: having shown the law is not abrogated, Q now takes up the Christians' positive charge — that the Torah contains no doctrine of eternal otherworldly reward and punishment (al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb al-abadī) — which Bab 7 will refute from Scripture.

- The catalogue→refutation architecture. Bab 6 is the delivery of the promise made in Bab 5: every prooftext catalogued there is taken up here in the same order — Trinitarian/Christological (§§2-7), then anti-legal (§§8-12), then the "already fulfilled" cluster (§§13-18). Bab 5 and Bab 6 must be read as a single argumentative unit; many of Bab 6's refutations presuppose that the reader has the Bab 5 catalogue in view (Q rarely re-quotes the Christian claim in full).

- Two registers of refutation. §1 distinguishes the rational refutation (already done in Babs 1-4, on the incoherence of tathlīth/ittiḥād) from the exegetical-philological refutation that is Bab 6's specific contribution. Almost every section turns on Hebrew lexicography: naʿaseh as plural-of-majesty (§2), ʿad as "when/since" (§3), ʿalmah as "young woman" (§4), rûaḥ as "command/prophecy" (§4 end), ben as "client/beloved" (§6), yikkaret as cessation-or-judicial-execution-but-never-unjust-killing (§13), and unqualified ʿarel as bodily-not-heart foreskin (§15). This is the Karaite philological method (peshaṭ / ẓāhir priority) deployed against Christian typology exactly as Q deploys it against Rabbanite midrash.

- The eschatological master-argument. The single most-repeated move in §§11, 14-18 is the appeal to the future-temple prophecies (especially Ezekiel 40-48, Isa 52, Isa 65-66, Jer 31, Zech 14): the redeemed age retains sacrifice, festivals, dietary law, and circumcision — therefore the law is not abrogated, and (a fortiori) the redemption has not yet occurred. This double-duty argument simultaneously refutes the anti-legal and the realized-eschatology Christian claims, and it is the structural backbone of the bab's second half.

- The Yashūʿ Paddā anecdote (§16) is one of the very few first-person disputation reports in the Anwār and is of real historical value: it attests live Karaite–East-Syrian-Christian debate in the ʿUkbarā/Baghdad milieu in Q's lifetime (first half of the 10th c.). The unidentified source-name לְאַדְרָא is a crux: the dialectic only works if it is the sole witness both to the post-exilic weeping and to the very fact of the Second Temple's rebuilding — pointing to a narrative/chronistic source (the Ezra-Nehemiah material, or an Aramaic Diatessaron-adjacent or apocryphal "record"). Left transliterated in the translation; flagged for the edition's notes.

- The Muslim-rule argument (§§14-15). Q twice uses the contemporary political fact of Muslim control of Jerusalem as an empirical disproof of realized eschatology — and pointedly frames it through Christian contempt for Islam ("the worst of God's creation in religion, on your view"). This dates and situates the argument firmly in the ʿAbbāsid present and shows Q willing to enlist a shared Jewish–Christian discomfort with the third party to score against the Christians.

- Cross-references to "the other / last book." Q three times (§3, §9, §12) defers exhaustive treatment to al-kitāb al-akhīr / al-kitāb al-ākhar and "the commentary on Bereshit" — i.e., his Torah commentary (Kitāb al-Riyāḍ wa-l-Ḥadāʾiq) and his anti-Mujbira free-will discussion. These confirm the Anwār was conceived as part of a larger, cross-referencing corpus.
